newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, Russian patriarch discuss religion bill.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Russian patriarch discuss religion bill.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin spoke by telephone on Friday with Patriarch Alexiy, head of the Russian Orthodox Church, in an effort to improve relations marred by recent disagreements over a controversial law on religion.

The presidential press service said in a statement that the two men had had "a cordial conversation" that focused on the draft law "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Associations" vetoed by Yeltsin last week.

Yeltsin rejected the bill, approved by both houses of parliament and strongly backed by the patriarch, because he said it contravened Russia's post-Soviet constitution guaranteeing equality for all faiths.
The bill, which drew strong criticism from the United States, the Vatican and human rights groups, would have imposed tough curbs on "non-traditional" religious groups in Russia.
Supporters of the bill said it would clamp down on the many religious sects that have flourished in post-communist Russia, exploiting people's spiritual hunger, naivety and poverty.
Sounding a conciliatory note on Friday, Yeltsin said he shared the patriarch's concern about the sects and said he was confident the government could counter their influence.
"The president and the patriarch agreed that the adoption of the law was necessary once the specific corrections...had been made," the Kremlin statement said.
Yeltsin has generally enjoyed good relations with the Church and has tried to use its spiritual authority and colourful symbolism to bolster his own position in the post-communist era.

Friday's statement praised the Church's central role in Russia's 1,000-year history and noted that much had been done in recent years to restore Church property and safeguard the rights of believers after the persecution of Soviet times.
Yeltsin and Alexiy agreed to cooperate closely in the reworking of the draft law, the statement said.
In separate comments on Friday, Alexiy expressed concern about what he called a "broad anti-Orthodox campaign unleashed by followers of pseudo-religious organisations", Itar-Tass news agency said.
